n: Nehemiah tells his own story, much like a personal journal. It is late in the year 445 BC, and he is serving in the Persian winter palace at Susa, about thirteen years after Ezra went to Jerusalem.

f.g: The twentieth year of King Artaxerxes I, about 445 BC (Nehemiah 2:1).
Susa, a royal capital of Persia in what is now southwestern Iran; also the setting of Esther.

n: Visitors arrive from Judah, including Nehemiah’s brother Hanani. Though Nehemiah has a comfortable life at court, his first question is about his people and the holy city.

f.g: Those who survived the exile and returned to Judah.

n: The news is grim: the returned exiles are struggling and mocked, and Jerusalem’s walls and gates still lie in ruins. Without walls, a city was defenseless and disgraced.

f.w: the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down

n: Nehemiah weeps, mourns, fasts, and prays for days. Before doing anything, he takes the problem to God. Four months pass before he speaks to the king (Nehemiah 2:1).
Nehemiah begins by praising God as great, awe-inspiring, and faithful to His covenant. He reminds himself whom he is speaking to before he asks for anything.
He asks God to listen, then confesses Israel’s sins — and includes himself and his own family. Like Ezra and Daniel, he does not point fingers but shares the blame.

f.w: both I and my father's house have sinned

n: Nehemiah admits plainly that Israel failed to keep the law given through Moses.
Now he appeals to God’s own word. Moses had warned that disobedience would bring scattering — and that warning came true.

f.w: I will scatter you abroad among the nations

n: But Moses also promised that if Israel returned to the Lord, He would gather them again, even from the ends of the earth. Nehemiah is praying in faith on a promise. Latter-day Saints see this same promise being fulfilled in the gathering of Israel today.

f.w: the place that I have chosen to set my name there

n: Nehemiah reminds God that these are still His people, whom He redeemed from Egypt with His mighty hand. Redemption is a covenant word: God had bought them back as His own.

He closes with a specific request: success “this day” when he approaches the king. Only now do we learn that Nehemiah is the king’s cupbearer — a trusted official close to the most powerful man in the world.

f.g: The king, Artaxerxes — great to the world, but just “this man” before God.
The official who served and tasted the king’s wine, guarding against poison; a highly trusted adviser.
